relevance_reason: Defines the SMARCA1-related X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder with variable macrocephaly. It reports 35 patients from 26 families, the variants, a methylation profile, functional studies and mouse models.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) described an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by de novo or maternally inherited SMARCA1 variants in 35 individuals from 26 families. Features ranged from mild to severe intellectual disability/developmental delay and included delayed or regressive speech, autism spectrum disorder features, facial dysmorphism and other variable features. Individuals with truncating variants had a high penetrance of macrocephaly.
quotes: Here, we describe 35 individuals from 26 families with de novo or maternally inherited variants in the X-linked SMARCA1 gene. This SMARCA1-related NDD is associated with a spectrum of involvement, including mild to severe ID/DD, delayed or regressive speech development, ASD features, facial dysmorphisms, and other variable features.
Individuals carrying SMARCA1 truncating variants exhibit a mildly unique genome-wide DNA methylation profile and a high penetrance of macrocephaly.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) studied a 6-generation family with 4 affected individuals who had mild to severe ID/DD and brain overgrowth. The proband, a 12-year-old boy, had head circumference (OFC) +6 SD, severe ID without language, ASD, hydrocephalus treated with a shunt, hepatosplenomegaly, and height and weight +5 SD. His brother had OFC +4.3 SD, mild ID, hydrocephalus and splenomegaly. Two maternal cousins (a 14-year-old girl and an 8-year-old boy) had OFC +4.9 and +5.5 SD, mild learning disability, obesity and normal brain MRI. Their carrier mothers had OFC +1 and +1.5 SD and no learning disability.
quotes: Our initial characterization began with performing exome sequencing on a large six-generation family (Fig. 1A) containing 4 individuals with mild to severe ID/DD and brain overgrowth.

Family 1 (DB17-332) (vi8) | F | 14y7m | c.271 C > T, p.Arg91* | Maternal | OFC + 4.9 SD | – | – | Mild LD | – | + (subtle) | Severe obesity (BMI 50 kg/m2), normal brain MRI

findings.statement: In the 4 affected members of the 6-generation family, Mirzaa et al. (2025) used exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous or heterozygous nonsense variant in SMARCA1, c.271C-T (p.Arg91Ter). Both mothers were heterozygous carriers, and the paternal grandfather and a maternal uncle did not carry the variant. The same variant was found in a second, unrelated family (family 2): a 6-year-old boy with macrocephaly, ASD and ADHD who had inherited it from his mother.
quotes: This study identified a hemizygous nonsense variant (c.271 C > T [p.Arg91*]) in the SMARCA1 gene (NM_003069.4) in the proband (vi1), his brother (vi2) and two maternal cousins (vi8 and vi9).
Both mothers (v2 and v10) of the affected individuals were heterozygous for the variant while the paternal grandfather (iv1) and maternal uncle (v5) were negative.
Family 2 (DB20-184) | M | 6 y | c.271 C > T, p.Arg91* | Maternal | Macrocephaly | + | + | + | ASD, ADHD + | + (subtle) | –

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) reported 35 affected individuals (26 males, 9 females) aged 2 to 49 years. Features were ID/DD (27/35), speech delay and/or regression (29/35), OFC of +2 SD or more and/or reported macrocephaly (17/35), motor delay (20/34), seizures (8/35), hypotonia (15/35), behavioral difficulties (19/35), ASD (11/35) and dysmorphic facial features (19/35). Height of +2 SD or more was less frequent (29%), which the authors said argued against a generalized overgrowth syndrome. Common facial features were frontal bossing, a long face, slanted palpebral fissures, a flat nasal root with a short bulbous nose, anteverted nares and a thin upper lip.
quotes: Most individuals presented with ID/DD (77%; 27/35) and speech delay and/or speech regression (83%; 29/35).

Other commonly reported clinical features included motor delay (20/34; 59%), seizures/epilepsy (23%; 8/35), and hypotonia (42%; 15/35). Over half the individuals (19/35; 54%) were diagnosed with behavioral difficulties (ASD, ADHD, aggression) and in some instances (9/25) this was linked to regression in speech and mental development.

Photographs from seven affected individuals show that frontal bossing, a long face, slanted palpebral fissures, a flat nasal root with a short bulbous nose, anteverted nares, and a thin upper lip were relatively common features of the cohort (Fig. 2).

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) noted other recurring features in the cohort. These included urogenital/kidney anomalies (9 individuals), gastrointestinal problems (9), eye/vision deficits (8) and hepatomegaly/splenomegaly (3). Recurrent dysmorphic features included ear anomalies (11 individuals) and micrognathia (5).
quotes: 3Other recurring features included urogenital/kidney (9 individuals), epilepsy/seizures (8), gastrointestinal problems (9), eye/vision deficits (8), hepatomegaly/splenomegaly (3).
2Recurrent dysmorphic features included ear anomalies (11 individuals), micrognathia (5), slanted palpebral fissures (5), prominent forehead (4), anteverted nostrils (4), bulbous nasal tip (3).

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) reported that, of the 26 index cases, 17 had maternally inherited SMARCA1 variants and 4 had de novo variants. Segregation was not determined in 5, of which 4 were presumed maternal. Three-quarters of affected individuals were hemizygous males; heterozygous females made up 25% and often had milder phenotypes, consistent with X-linked inheritance.
quotes: Within the 26 index cases, 17 had a maternally inherited variant, four variants occurred de novo, and for five cases the segregation was not determined, although four of these were presumed maternally inherited.

Three quarters of the affected individuals described were hemizygous males, most with maternally inherited variants. Heterozygous females comprised the remaining 25% of affected cases, and these individuals often showed a milder phenotype.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) identified 9 affected females, 7 of whom had truncating variants; 3 of these 7 had macrocephaly and 4 did not. Macrocephaly was discordant in 2 mother-daughter pairs, and learning disabilities appeared milder in females. X-inactivation studies were available for only 3 females and did not match the phenotype.
quotes: Nine 9 affected females were identified in our cohort, including 7 with truncating variants. Females with truncating variants were evenly split between those with macrocephaly (3) and those without (4).
Many of these effects could be attributed to differences in X-inactivation skewing, but such studies were only available from three females, and they were discordant with phenotype.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found macrocephaly in 70% of individuals with truncating variants. However, 3 individuals with truncating variants lacked brain overgrowth and 4 with missense variants had it, so the feature was not restricted to putative loss-of-function variants. Individuals with CNV deletions that included SMARCA1 did not have macrocephaly. Three of the 4 missense variants associated with macrocephaly were in the HSS domain.
quotes: However, amongst individuals with truncating variants, the penetrance of macrocephaly was 70% suggesting that a straight LOF mechanism does not result in macrocephaly.

However, three individuals with truncating variants without brain overgrowth and four individuals with missense variants with brain overgrowth suggest that this feature is more complex and not restricted to individuals with putative LOF variants.

Three of four missense variants associated with macrocephaly are in the HSS domain, which may prevent remodeling activity and could lead to dominant-negative effects on gene expression, similar to the Smarca1ex6del mice.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) identified the SMARCA1 variants by trio exome sequencing (23 families) or genome sequencing (3 families), with families ascertained partly through MatchMaker Exchange. There were 25 unique variants: 7 nonsense, 3 frameshift and 15 missense. All were predicted deleterious, and each was very rare or absent in gnomAD (allele frequency 8.303 x 10(-7) or lower; p.Met432Thr was seen in 4 alleles). Sixteen variants were in the ATPase (12) or HSS (4) domains.
quotes: Pathogenic variants were identified in SMARCA1 using a combination of trio-based exome sequencing (ES; 23 families), short read whole genome sequencing (WGS; 3 families) in both clinical diagnostic and research settings.

This analysis identified several single reports (allele frequency ≤8.303 × 10−7) while the c.1295 T > C,p.Met432Thr variant was present in four alleles but with an equally low allele frequency (≤3.4 × 10−6; see Supplementary Table 2).
Sixteen of the 25 unique variants identified resided within these two functional domains (12 in ATPase, 4 in HSS) while a previously reported case (p.Gly966Val) is also located in the HSS domain.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) considered SMARCA1 variants in 7 additional families likely non-causative. These included p.Val384Met (c.1150G-A) in 3 families; this variant had previously been reported in familial schizophrenia and was present in gnomAD in 16 alleles, including 7 hemizygotes. Others were p.Pro537Leu (c.1610C-T) in 2 families, which also had a high gnomAD frequency, and p.Gly38Val, found together with a de novo 5p15 duplication.
quotes: This cohort included three families with the same variant (c.1150 G > A,p.Val384Met) that has previously been reported in a pedigree of familial schizophrenia and co-segregated with a variant in the AVEN gene, drawing into question the causality of this variant.
Moreover, this variant was present in gnomAD in 16/1195462 alleles in presumably healthy individuals, including 7 hemizygotes (allele frequency 0.00001338; see SupplementaryTable 2).
Two other families had an identical variant (c.1610 C > T, p.Pro537Leu) that was similarly present with a high allele frequency in gnomAD.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) searched DECIPHER and found 72 CNVs encompassing SMARCA1 (44% deletions, 56% duplications). Carriers often had developmental delay, intellectual disability or delayed speech, but the phenotype was hard to attribute to SMARCA1 because most CNVs were larger than 10 Mb. Individuals with deletions did not have macrocephaly.
quotes: Publicly available data identified 72 CNVs with an almost equal-split between deletions (44%) and duplications (56%).
Similarly, individuals with CNV deletions encompassing the SMARCA1 gene were not associated with macrocephaly.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) performed genome-wide DNA methylation analysis of peripheral blood from 19 individuals with SMARCA1 variants and found a predominantly hypomethylated profile defined by 232 probes compared with controls. Males and females each also showed sex-specific hypomethylated profiles. The authors concluded that these changes were not robust enough to count as an episignature.
quotes: Initial analysis of all 19 individuals compared to 57 controls matched by age, sex and array type revealed a predominantly hypomethylated profile defined by 232 probes differentiating cases from controls (Fig. 3A).

While we demonstrated evidence of a mild global DNA methylation profile shared by patients with truncating variants and overgrowth, these changes were not sufficiently robust to be considered an epi-signature at this time

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) expressed FLAG-tagged SMARCA1 variants in U2OS cells. The p.Arg253Ter, p.Arg259Gly, p.Arg751Gln and p.Glu771Lys variants all produced stable proteins that localized to the nucleus. The Arg253Ter variant produced a stable 35-kD truncated protein at a somewhat lower level, and it was also found in the cytoplasm. The authors suggested that some truncating variants generate truncated proteins with hypomorphic or dominant-negative activity.
quotes: Following transfection, we observed that all 4 variants produced a stable protein, including the R253* variant which generated a protein of 35 kDa in size, albeit at a somewhat lower protein level than the other variants (Fig. 5A).

The exogenous expression of the p.Arg253* truncating variant in U2OS cells generated a truncated 35 kDa SMARCA1 protein that was stable and partially mislocalized to the cytoplasm, thereby suggesting that some truncating variants may generate truncated proteins with hypomorphic or dominant-negative activity.

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found that Smarca1-null mice were viable and had little change in brain size, only slight reductions in a few regions, with normal progenitor populations and cortical lamination. The mice were more active in the dark cycle but otherwise behaved normally on tests of locomotion, social interaction, anxiety, learning and memory. In Smarca1-null cerebellum, SMARCA5 co-immunoprecipitated with CECR2, which the authors suggested reflects functional compensation by SMARCA5.
quotes: Taken together, we conclude that the Smarca1 KO mice do not present with a brain overgrowth phenotype or with major deficits in forebrain development, which is in stark contrast to the phenotype of the Smarca1ex6del mice and many individuals of the SMARCA1 cohort with truncating variants.

Overall, the Smarca1 KO mice were more active in the dark but otherwise, this battery of behavior tests did not identify any statistically significant differences between the Smarca1 KO mice and their littermate controls
However, in Smarca1 KO lysates, the SMARCA5 antibody was able to co-IP the CECR2 protein, suggesting that it functionally compensates for the loss of SMARCA1 protein (Fig. 8C, lower panel).

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) compared single and double knockouts of the NURF components Smarca1, Smarca5 and Bptf in mice. Bptf knockout caused the most severe cortical hypoplasia, and no double mutant was more severe. Smarca1ex6del mice, which express an internally truncated protein, had a total brain area 10% larger than controls, but this enlargement was lost when Smarca5 was also ablated. The authors proposed that Smarca5 compensates for complete loss of Smarca1 but not when a mutant SMARCA1 protein is produced, which may act as a dominant negative.
quotes: This analysis showed that the total brain area of the Smarca1ex6del mice was 10% larger than controls (SupplementaryFig. 4), which was not fully reflected in the cortical area measurements, where we observed a 1% increase.

Taken together, these data reveal that proper cortical development requires NURF, and that Smarca5 fully compensates when Smarca1 is completely ablated (no difference in brain size in Smarca1 KO) but not when some SMARCA1 protein is produced (e.g. Smarca1ex6del mice).

findings.statement: Mirzaa et al. (2025) proposed that SMARCA1 variants associated with macrocephaly lack remodeling activity and act in a dominant-negative fashion, whereas variants not associated with macrocephaly may be functional hypomorphs. In their view, all of these variants alter NURF composition and function in the developing brain.
quotes: Individuals with SMARCA1 variants and macrocephaly are predicted to lack remodeling activity and function in a dominant negative fashion, while variants not associated with macrocephaly are predicted to be functional hypomorphs.

Regardless, the genetic mechanism(s) causing the SMARCA1-related NDD is complex and may be variant dependent, yet we predict that they all impact NURF composition and NURF function in the developing brain.

relevance_reason: Reports two male patients with XLID and hemizygous SMARCA1 variants, with macrocephaly in one, directly characterizing NEDMAC.

findings.statement: Nishimura et al. (2025) reported 2 unrelated male patients with X-linked intellectual disability. Patient 1 had macrocephaly, behavioral difficulty, and learning disability; patient 2 had ataxia and speech delay.
quotes: Here, we report two unrelated male patients with XLID due to novel SMARCA1 variants detected by exome sequencing.
Patient 1 showed macrocephaly, behavioral difficulty, and learning disability
Patient 2 had ataxia and speech delay

findings.statement: In a male patient (patient 1) with X-linked intellectual disability, macrocephaly, behavioral difficulty, and learning disability, Nishimura et al. (2025) identified by exome sequencing a hemizygous nonsense variant in the SMARCA1 gene (c.1795C-T, Gln599Ter; NM_003069.5) that led to nonsense-mediated decay. The variant was inherited from his unaffected mother.
quotes: Patient 1 showed macrocephaly, behavioral difficulty, and learning disability with a hemizygous SMARCA1 variant (NM_003069.5:c.1795 C > T p.[Gln599*]) leading to nonsense-mediated decay.
Both variants were inherited from their unaffected healthy mothers.

findings.statement: In a male patient (patient 2) with X-linked intellectual disability, ataxia, and speech delay, Nishimura et al. (2025) identified by exome sequencing a hemizygous missense variant in the SMARCA1 gene (c.1343G-T, Arg448Leu; NM_003069.5), inherited from his unaffected mother. Structural modeling suggested that Arg448Leu might destabilize interactions between SMARCA1 and nucleosomal DNA.

findings.statement: Nishimura et al. (2025) found that the SMARCA1 variants in both affected males were inherited from unaffected healthy mothers. They suggested that hemizygous variants impairing SMARCA1 function can cause XLID with variable features in males.
quotes: Both variants were inherited from their unaffected healthy mothers.
This study suggests that hemizygous variants impairing SMARCA1 function can cause XLID with other variable features, such as macrocephaly and ataxia, in men.

relevance_reason: This large exome-sequencing study of consanguineous Pakistani families with recessive intellectual disability lists novel candidate genes. These include a TMEM222 missense variant in family PKMR213, which would be relevant to a TMEM222-related neurodevelopmental disorder. The paper does not name NEDMAC or say which gene causes it; linking NEDMAC to TMEM222 is an assumption.

findings.statement: Riazuddin et al. (2017) carried out exome sequencing in 121 consanguineous Pakistani families with autosomal recessive intellectual disability. In a Siraiki Baloch family (PKMR213), they found a variant in the novel candidate gene TMEM222 (NM_032125.2), c.214G>A (p.Gly72Ser), that segregated with the phenotype. The variant had a CADD score of 34.0 and an ExAC allele frequency of 8.237 x 10(-6), and it was absent from 213 ethnically matched controls.
quotes: PKMR213 | Siraiki Baloch | TMEM222 | Chr1:27657230G>A | NM_032125.2 | c.214G>A | p.(Gly72Ser) | Missense | Transmembrane protein | 34.0 | 8.237
In 30 families we identified plausible pathogenic variants affecting a single gene that had not been previously implicated in ARID (Table 2; Supplementary Figure S4).
None of the variants were found in 213 unrelated, ethnically matched control individuals, indicating that they are not indigenous Pakistani polymorphisms.

findings.statement: Lopes et al. (2016) studied 19 Portuguese patients (16 girls and 3 boys) whose clinical presentation overlapped significantly with Rett syndrome. The patients were studied with array CGH, whole-exome sequencing, MRI and muscle biopsy.
quotes: We studied a cohort of 19 Portuguese patients (16 girls, 3 boys) with a clinical presentation significantly overlapping Rett syndrome (RTT).
Examination by MRI and muscle biopsies was also performed.

findings.statement: In a cohort of 19 Portuguese patients with Rett-like phenotypes, Lopes et al. (2016) used whole-exome sequencing to find variants in 5 novel candidate neurodevelopmental disorder genes (26% of patients). These were de novo variants in RHOBTB2, SMARCA1 and GABBR2, a homozygous variant in EIF4G1, and compound heterozygous variants in HTT. Network analysis showed that these genes interact through protein interactions with each other and with the known Rett syndrome genes.
quotes: Variants were also detected in five novel NDD candidate genes (26%): we identified de novo variants in the RHOBTB2, SMARCA1 and GABBR2 genes; a homozygous variant in EIF4G1; compound heterozygous variant in HTT.
Network analysis reveals that these genes interact by means of protein interactions with each other and with the known RTT genes.

findings.statement: Lopes et al. (2016) found variants in genes already linked to neurodevelopmental disorders in 6 of 19 patients (32%) with Rett-like phenotypes. Three patients had de novo variants in EEF1A2, STXBP1 or ZNF238. Two male patients had maternally inherited X-linked variants in SLC35A2, ZFX and SHROOM4. One patient had a homozygous EIF2B2 variant. Pathogenic genomic imbalances were found in 2 further patients: an 18q21.2 deletion that included 4 exons of TCF4, and mosaic uniparental disomy of chromosome 3.
quotes: de novo variants in EEF1A2, STXBP1 and ZNF238 were found in three patients, maternally inherited X linked variants in SLC35A2, ZFX and SHROOM4 were detected in two male patients and one homozygous variant in EIF2B2 was detected in one patient.
Pathogenic genomic imbalances were found in two patients (10.5%): an 18q21.2 deletion encompassing four exons of the TCF4 gene and a mosaic UPD of chromosome 3.

relevance_reason: Large exome-sequencing cohort of neurogenetic disorders. One patient had a hemizygous SMARCA1 nonsense variant with microcephaly, intellectual disability and Coffin-Siris-like features, which is early supporting evidence for an SMARCA1-related neurodevelopmental disorder. The link between SMARCA1 and this entry is an assumption: the entry header does not name a gene.

findings.statement: Karaca et al. (2015) described a male patient (BAB4453) with microcephaly, spasticity and intellectual disability. He had dysmorphic features resembling Coffin-Siris syndrome, including a coarse face, bushy eyebrows, facial hypertrichosis and long eyelashes. Brain imaging showed severe cortical atrophy. Family history was negative.
quotes: Patient BAB4453 presented with microcephaly, spasticity, and intellectual disability. He also had very similar dysmorphic features similar to those seen in Coffin-Siris syndrome (MIM# 135900) (Figure 6C). Family history was negative.

BAB4453 with homozygous stop gain (p.Q3X) in SMARCA1 represents severe cortical atrophy. Patient image underlines the coarse face, bushy eyebrows, facial hypertrichosis, and long eye lashes which resembles the facial dysmorphism in Coffin-Siris syndrome.

findings.statement: In a male patient (BAB4453) with microcephaly, spasticity, intellectual disability and Coffin-Siris-like dysmorphic features, Karaca et al. (2015) used whole exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous null variant in the SMARCA1 gene (c.C7T, p.Q3X; NM_003069). SMARCA1 encodes a member of the SWI/SNF protein family and is part of the ATP-dependent CECR2-containing remodeling factor (CERF). A figure legend in the paper calls the same variant a homozygous stop gain.
quotes: He was found to have a hemizygous null variant in the SMARCA1 gene (NM_003069: c.C7T, p.Q3X) (Tables 1A and S1, Figure 6C), which encodes a member of the SWI/SNF family of proteins and is part of the ATP-dependent CECR2-containing remodeling factor (CERF) (Figure 6C).
BAB4453 with homozygous stop gain (p.Q3X) in SMARCA1 represents severe cortical atrophy.
